kit.name: ELEGOO UNO R3 Super Starter Kit

identity.manufacturer: generic, widely cloned part number; the datasheet fetched is from XLITX Technology, but the same 3461BS numbering and pinout is used by many Chinese LED display makers
generic_equivalents: other 0.36 inch 4-digit common-anode displays with the same 12-pin layout
identity.package: 12-pin through-hole DIP-style 4-digit 7-segment display, 0.36 inch (9.2 mm) digit height

function.one_sentence_plain_english: Four 7-segment digits in a row, wired so the Arduino lights them one at a time so fast it looks like all four glow at once.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Used to show numbers with more than one digit, like a clock, a counter, or a temperature reading with a decimal point.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Each of the 4 digits is a copy of the same 8-LED figure-8 pattern. To save pins, the same 8 segment wires (a-g, dp) are shared by all 4 digits; only one digit's common pin is active at a time (this is the common-anode version, so 'active' means driving that digit's common pin HIGH). The Arduino rapidly cycles through digit 1, 2, 3, 4, showing the right number on each one for a few milliseconds. It happens faster than the eye can see, so it looks like a steady 4-digit number. This trick is called multiplexing.

pins.pin_1_identification: Confirmed from the datasheet's dimension diagram: hold the display face-up in normal reading orientation (decimal points along the bottom edge of each digit). Pin 1 is the leftmost pin on the front (bottom) row of legs.

electrical.operating_voltage: each digit's common (anode) pin is driven near 5V when that digit is selected; segments sink current to a low logic level through a resistor when lit
electrical.typical_current: 10 mA per segment (datasheet test condition); multiplexed use commonly runs briefly higher pulsed current per segment to keep brightness up while lit only 1/4 of the time
electrical.max_current: 30 mA continuous per segment; 200 mA peak per segment at 1/10 duty cycle, 10 kHz (datasheet absolute maximum ratings)
electrical.logic_level: 5V logic; needs current-limiting resistors on the 8 segment lines (commonly 220-330 ohm), and may need a transistor per digit if the total current exceeds what an Arduino pin can safely supply

visual_identification.shape_and_size: Black rectangular plastic housing about 30 mm wide and 14 mm tall, with four separate figure-8 shaped red display windows in a row, each with its own small decimal point dot at the bottom-right. Twelve thin metal legs come out the bottom, 6 per row, front and back.
visual_identification.color_and_markings: Black plastic body, red segments. Usually no printed model number visible on the part.
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: Usually none; if present, look for '3461' as the model family. Four separate digit windows in a row is the main visual giveaway versus the single-digit part.
easily_confused_with: the 1-digit 7-segment display in this kit (same color scheme, but only one window instead of four)
an LED dot-matrix module (also a black rectangle with red LEDs, but arranged as a dot grid, not bar segments)

example_connections.uno_pin: digital pin, e.g. D9, selects the leftmost digit
digital pin, e.g. D2, through a 220-330 ohm resistor
digital pin, e.g. D10, selects the second digit

required_extra_parts: one 220-330 ohm resistor per segment line (up to 8 total)
optionally 4 small NPN or PNP transistors if driving digits needs more current than the Arduino pins can safely supply
wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: none required for basic multiplexing written by hand in a loop; the SevSeg library is commonly used to simplify driving it

handling_notes: always use series resistors on the segment lines
when multiplexing, never drive more than one digit's common pin HIGH at the same instant, or the digits will bleed light into each other
common_mistakes: wiring it as if it were common cathode (this part is common anode: digit pins must be driven HIGH to select a digit, and segments pulled LOW to light, the opposite of a common-cathode display)
refreshing the digits too slowly in code, causing visible flicker

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: only one digit ever lights up, or the same digit repeats across all four positions
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: digit-select pins (6, 8, 9, 12) wired or coded incorrectly, or the sketch never cycles through the other digits
symptoms_and_causes.check: verify each DIG pin goes to a separate Arduino pin and the sketch loops through all four digits in sequence

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: display looks dim or flickers badly
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: the multiplexing loop refreshes too slowly, or resistor values are too high
symptoms_and_causes.check: increase the refresh rate in code (aim for each digit redrawn at least ~100 times per second total) and confirm resistors are 220-330 ohm

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: segments seem inverted, dim ones look 'on' and bright ones look 'off'
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: code written for a common-cathode display applied to this common-anode part
symptoms_and_causes.check: confirm HIGH on a DIG pin selects that digit and LOW on a segment pin lights that segment, not the reverse

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: Set a multimeter to its diode-test function. Touch the positive probe to a DIG pin (6, 8, 9, or 12) and the negative probe to a segment pin (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10, or 11); the matching segment on that digit should light up dimly, confirming both the pin map and that this part is common anode.

confidence.notes: Every US-based retailer fetch attempted (Amazon x2, Abra Electronics) failed or returned no usable pricing, so the single-unit retail price is taken from a South African electronics shop and converted to USD at an approximate September 2026 rate (~18.3 ZAR/USD). That listing independently confirmed the exact part number (3461BS) and common-anode configuration, matching the datasheet. The manufacturer's own bulk factory price ($0.76 per 100-piece minimum order from XLITX) is far lower per unit than any real single-piece retail price and was not used as the headline number for that reason, though the datasheet from that same source was used for all pin and electrical specs.
